nameStory: The Norway King Crab gets its royal title from its impressive size and spiny armor that makes it look like it's wearing a crown of thorns. Despite being called the 'Norway' crab, this cold-water royalty actually rules territories on both sides of the North Atlantic, from the fjords of Scandinavia to the rocky coasts of New England.
description: The Norway King Crab is a heavily armored crustacean that looks like something from a medieval fantasy tale. Its almost perfectly circular shell, called a carapace, can grow as wide as a dinner plate - up to about 5-6 inches across. The entire crab is covered in large, intimidating spikes and comes in rich brown or bright orange colors that help it blend with rocky sea floors.

idTips.label: Spiky armor plating
idTips.description: The entire body is covered with large, sharp spikes that feel like thorns - handle with thick gloves! These aren't small bumps but substantial spines that give the crab a fierce, medieval armor appearance.

idTips.label: Circular shell shape
idTips.description: The carapace is almost perfectly round, like a spiky dinner plate, rather than the more oval or triangular shapes of most other crabs you'll find in New England waters.

idTips.label: Brown to orange coloration
idTips.description: Look for rich, earthy colors ranging from deep chocolate brown to bright pumpkin orange - never the dull gray-green of common shore crabs.

idTips.label: Asymmetrical abdomen in females
idTips.description: Female crabs have a noticeably lopsided underside, with the left side of the belly flap much larger than the right - an unusual trait that's easy to spot when you flip them over.

idTips.label: Substantial size
idTips.description: These are hefty crabs that feel surprisingly heavy in your hands - much more solid and robust than the lightweight rock crabs commonly found in tide pools.

habitat: In New England waters, Norway King Crabs live in deep, cold offshore areas rather than the shallow tide pools where most people look for crabs. They prefer depths of 30 feet to over 3,000 feet, living on both soft muddy bottoms and hard rocky surfaces along the continental shelf.

seasonality.spring: Deep-water species rarely seen in shallow areas, but commercial fishermen and deep-sea researchers may encounter them as waters begin to warm.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to spot one if brought up by fishing gear or research vessels, as this is peak season for deep-water activities.
seasonality.fall: Occasionally found in deeper tide pools during extreme low tides, though still very rare in accessible areas.
seasonality.winter: Remains active in deep, cold waters while most shallow-water crabs become dormant, but virtually impossible to observe from shore.

funFact: Female Norway King Crabs are natural lefties - their left side is dramatically bigger than their right side, making them one of the most lopsided creatures in the ocean, though occasionally you'll find a rare 'righty' with the opposite arrangement!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded sighting in New England, you're more likely to confuse a spiky sea urchin shell or a piece of spiny driftwood for this crab than to actually find one! If you think you've found one, you've probably discovered something much more common like a rock crab or jonah crab.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'crab,' king crabs are actually more closely related to hermit crabs than true crabs - they're evolutionary cousins that developed similar body plans independently. This explains some of their unique features, like the asymmetrical abdomen.
compareHints: Since there are no other Lithodes species in New England waters, compare this to other king crab relatives like hermit crabs, which share the asymmetrical abdomen but lack the heavily spined, circular carapace. Unlike the smooth-shelled or lightly bumpy crabs common in New England, the Norway King Crab's massive spines make it unmistakable if you ever encounter one.
